📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AC Milan put on a show at San Siro on Sunday night as they swept Frosinone aside emphatically, beating them 5-1.

The own-goal that Gabriele Calvani scored a few minutes in set the tone for the visitors, while Goncalo Ramos broke his drought after starting and finishing a counter-attack. However, Patrizio Masini’s goal shortly after meant the deficit was halved going into the break.

According to recent reports, read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

In the second half, Milan ran riot. Ardon Jashari and Alphadjo Cisse both had opportunities after being found in behind, and both just minutes after coming off the bench. Then, Christian Pulisic added the finishing touch to make it a five-star night.

It was a win that Milan needed, considering that only Inter out of the current top six, dropped points, and it moves the Rossoneri back into the top four spots. Ivan Stoev has picked out the key talking points from the game.

Technically, Rabiot won the MOTM in our post-game ratings, but we absolutely have to talk about Luka Modric.

According to recent reports, I’ve personally had my doubts about the Croatian being able to keep up this season, especially under Ruben Amorim. We all expected the Portuguese coach to bring a lot of intensity to Milan’s game and at times, Modric has seemed to struggle.

Maybe that was because of the team adapting to the new coach, or maybe the midfielder hadn’t completely recovered after the World Cup – who knows.

The reality is that the former Real Madrid man has stepped up after some shaky games at the start of the season and continues to prove his quality on and off the ball and his athleticism and longevity are nothing short of extraordinary.

Recent findings suggest that the vision and passing ability to play the through ball to Rabiot for the opening goal was world-class. He then continued to dictate the tempo and make impressive forward runs, playing the full 90 minutes, giving it his all until the final whistle.

The management really needs to assemble a whole group of people tasked to find a proper replacement for Modric, as he will leave a big gap in that midfield.

To continue with the midfielder theme, we also have to give praise to Rabiot, who has been absolutely brilliant this season. Don’t get me wrong, he was one of the Rossoneri’s best players last year too.

Yet he has found a higher level since the start of the campaign, as he racked up another two assists and forced the own goal. As a result, he now has five goals and seven assists in 10 games in Serie A – extraordinary numbers.

On top of the goal contributions, you can count on the Frenchman to be composed under pressure, tidy with his passing, and efficient in both phases of the game. An absolutely stunning start of the season for Rabiot, who is finding latest levels to his game under Amorim.

It was such a dominant win that we can probably cover each player and the positives from their game. Nevertheless, one man needs to be praised for sure and that’s Goncalo Ramos, who got himself back on the scoresheet.

Industry observers note that needless to say, he opened up a lot of spaces for his teammates and had a role in some of the other goals, which he was doing even when he failed to get the ball in the back of the net. This time around, he also got his long-awaited goal.

It was a beauty too, in the sense that he dropped deep into his own half, made the tackle to win the ball and kicked off the counter-attack. Following that, he made the run into the opponent’s box and finished it calmly – it was beautifully orchestrated with Ramos in the centre.

The goal and the encouraging performance are also a relief, as we’ve seen many times how strikers struggle to react when they are not scoring, with the confidence level often dropping which results in overall poor form.

However, the Portuguese striker is clearly not in his head and reacted well to a poor spell that spanned both his club and the national team, as he struggled in the international break too.

We didn’t even see that much of him as Amorim subbed him off rather early and it probably has to do with the fact that Milan need a win on Thursday against Olympiacos, in Greece, and Ramos will most likely start the game as the margin for error is little as things stand.

In a recent development, I mean, what more can you ask from your attackers? Diego Moreira got the hockey assist on the second goal and got an assist for Cisse in the second half and on top of that, was heavily involved and dangerous when the Diavolo went on the counter.

According to recent reports, truthfully, the Belgian should have probably scored a goal or two as he had some very good chances in the opponent’s penalty box, but his shooting let him down this time around. Nevertheless, another electric performance.

Speaking of electric – Pulisic also did very well as he was involved in the first goal – even if it ended up being an own goal, his run forced the Frosinone defender to run back and eventually put the ball in his own net.

The American then got his goal in the second half with a composed finish. He had a very solid game overall with lots of smart movements and combination play- nothing flashy, but the efficiency was there.

Then we also have Cisse, who started the game on the bench but only needed nine or so minutes after coming on to get his goal. Ridiculously, he now has six in 10 in the league or a goal every 74 minutes. The youngster made a good run and managed to keep himself onside in a tricky situation and then finished with composure.

The variety in attack by Milan on the night was a joy to watch, as all the players posed a threat to Frosinone, which in the end was too much for them to handle.

Amorim was well aware of how Frosinone would approach the game, which in itself deserves credit as they came to San Siro to play football instead of sitting back. Unfortunately for them and fortunately for us, the coach and his players knew exactly how to get around the high press.

The Rossoneri were rapid on the counter and created so many chances that the score could’ve easily been even worse for Frosinone. Their high press also didn’t work, as for the majority of the game the Diavolo managed to move the ball around rapidly enough, which prevented their opponents from winning it in dangerous areas.

It also must be said that the Portuguese did well to rest some key players after the third goal, as he will need a fresh lineup for the Europa League fixture on Thursday, where Milan need three points against Olympiacos.

A budget below £50m, alongside the expectation of only two additions, makes it difficult to see United addressing all three areas in January.

A move for someone like Lewis Hall at left-back or Branthwaite at centre-back would seemingly be beyond their financial reach, particularly if Newcastle and Everton demand substantial fees.

However, Balde and RB Leipzig's David Raum could represent more budget-friendly alternatives, depending on their respective clubs' willingness to negotiate.

Sources indicate that the bigger question is whether United can afford to strengthen centrally and up front as well. Collins could be a realistic defensive target, but finding the funds for another centre-back and a striker on top of that looks particularly difficult at this stage.

Unless United generate significant funds through player sales, Pochettino may have to prioritise two positions and make the best of the squad he inherits.

Industry observers note that calhanoglu’s output is real, but it comes with a decline in athleticism that a 33-year-old can’t reverse. Spurs would be paying for a short-term fix in a position where they have already invested £185m in the long-term answer.

Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta has warned Ethan Nwaneri that brief flashes of quality will not be enough to secure regular football at Borussia Dortmund.

The record-breaking 19-year-old joined the Bundesliga leaders on loan from the Gunners in the summer, but has struggled for opportunities in recent weeks.

Nwaneri could now face his parent club in Tuesday's Champions League meeting in north London, with Arteta making his expectations clear.

Nwaneri initially enjoyed opportunities in Niko Kovac's starting lineup after arriving in Germany, but his involvement has since diminished significantly.

The versatile attacking midfielder has not started a match in over a month and has played just five minutes across Dortmund's last three Bundesliga fixtures.

Arteta believes the teenager must show greater consistency to establish himself at the highest level, insisting that occasional impressive performances are not enough.

"We're talking here about the highest level in Europe," the Arsenal boss said (via the Evening Standard). "You can just shine in moments, but moments are not enough. Now you need to show the consistency.".

The Spaniard also stressed that Nwaneri must earn his place in a talented Dortmund squad, rather than expect opportunities because of his Arsenal background.

"He needs to earn the right to play," Arteta added, explaining that joining a major European club does not automatically guarantee minutes.

Arteta remains convinced that Nwaneri has the mentality and quality to succeed, but acknowledged that his loan spells at Marseille and Dortmund form part of a challenging development journey.

Arsenal are understood to have the option to recall the youngster in January if his situation does not improve, with Arteta presently unconvinced that the Dortmund move is delivering the desired benefits.

Nwaneri is eligible to feature against his parent club on Tuesday, although Dortmund's strong form makes a starting place appear unlikely.

Nevertheless, the opportunity to face Arsenal off the bench could provide the teenager with an ideal platform to respond to Arteta's comments, particularly after his recent lack of involvement.

The Gunners boss has challenged him to show consistency and earn his place, rather than rely on occasional moments of quality. A positive contribution against the Premier League champions would certainly help his case.

Should Nwaneri find the net, he could join a select group of players to score against their parent clubs while on loan, including James Rodriguez against Real Madrid and Philippe Coutinho against Barcelona during their respective spells at Bayern Munich.

It would be a significant way to make his mark, although simply earning meaningful minutes against Arsenal would represent an encouraging step in his Dortmund journey.

However, the club hierarchy are understood to remain keen to give their summer appointment time, although the next few fixtures could prove crucial.

Chelsea's board have no immediate plans to sack Alonso, but the 44-year-old is under pressure to deliver results in the coming matches, according to newly introduced reports.

The Blues face Nottingham Forest and Crystal Palace next, before a demanding run of fixtures against Liverpool, Manchester City and Aston Villa. The three matches before Christmas could "make or break" Alonso's future at Stamford Bridge.

Chelsea right now sit eighth in the Premier League table, with supporters having already voiced their frustration during the defeat to Leeds.

There are also concerns of a "mutiny" behind the scenes, with it believed that several players are unhappy with Alonso's coaching methods at the training ground and that there is a "terrible atmosphere in the dressing room".

Nevertheless, the hierarchy are understood to believe that injuries have contributed to the team's struggles. Joao Pedro has been absent since the middle of October with a thigh problem, having been an key figure earlier in the campaign.

The club are hopeful that his return could help spark an improvement in results, although the pressure on Alonso is unlikely to disappear unless performances improve.

Clearlake have made managerial changes a regular feature of their Chelsea project, but dismissing Alonso just months into his tenure would risk repeating a familiar cycle at Stamford Bridge.

The Spaniard is still relatively early into his reign and has had to contend with important absences, particularly Pedro and captain Reece James. Both are usual starters who could make a significant difference to the side, especially in a system that relies on their respective qualities.

The reported dressing-room discontent is concerning, however, and Alonso will need to address that quickly, but it should not automatically mean his position is untenable.

Recent findings suggest that managers need time to implement their ideas, build relationships and establish consistency. Chelsea have invested in Alonso and should allow him to demonstrate what he can achieve with a fitter squad.

The upcoming fixtures will undoubtedly test that patience, but another change of manager so early in the process would hardly represent a convincing long-term strategy.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 21:00 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 21:00 EST, 20 November 2026.
  • Some grounds take you to the heart of the English game.
  • But each of them holds the soul of their community and the hopes and dreams of the thousands of people who make the pilgrimage there every weekend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 21:00 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 21:00 EST, 20 November 2026.

Some grounds are beautiful. Some grounds are not so beautiful. Some grounds take you to the heart of the English game. And some leave you feeling like you're on the periphery.

But each of them holds the soul of their community and the hopes and dreams of the thousands of people who make the pilgrimage there every weekend.

In a recent development, on April 1, 2025, I made the trip to Harrogate Town’s Exercise Stadium and first fulfilled the quest of a lifetime by completing the set of all 92 English Football League grounds for Daily Mail Sport. But then Everton moved away from Goodison Park and into a stunning latest stadium on the banks of the River Mersey.

Sources indicate that I was one short again but on February 23, 2026, I got back up to 92 by going to Hill Dickinson Stadium to watch Everton versus Manchester United. Then, in November, with York City being promoted (alongside Rochdale, whose ground I had ticked off decades ago), I made the trip to the LNER Stadium to make the 92 whole again.

I won’t give too much away just yet, but why are grounds like AFC Wimbledon and Exeter City in my top 20? What about Anfield, Old Trafford and Stamford Bridge? Where does Everton’s dazzling new home rank? Where is the best grub in the Premier League and where did Tyson Fury once threaten to have my jaw broken?

It has been revealed that this is my love letter to English football. Read on to find out who comes out on top, where your team ranks and everything else in between – then let me know what you think of my guide to the 92 grounds of England.

Division: Championship Opened: 1993 Capacity: 19,369.

Being banned from The Den is the football equivalent of being banned from your local abattoir.

In a recent development, I’ve been banned from The Den for the last 20 months, in a professional capacity anyway. I could still go in a personal capacity but, on balance, I think I’d rather not.

The Daily Mail has been told that our reporters are not welcome at the club because we had the temerity to report on the horrendous challenge by Millwall goalkeeper Liam Roberts on Crystal Palace’s Jean-Philippe Mateta during the FA Cup tie at Selhurst Park in March last year, which left the French striker requiring 25 stitches in his left ear.

Sources indicate that let’s be honest about this: there are worse places to be banned from. Being banned from The Den is the football equivalent of being banned from your local abattoir. You don’t have to be a racist, misogynistic, homophobic bloke with anger complications and a penchant for tragedy-chanting to feel at home at The Den. But it helps.

And, yes, I know Millwall are trying to rebrand themselves as a ‘family club’ now and the odd Tarquin and Tabitha stray across the county lines from Blackheath and Clapham to keep it real but that just makes The Den experience even worse.

The last time I went as a supporter was 16 years ago to watch Stockport County play there and the walk from South Bermondsey station to the away turnstiles was an eye-opener.

Not that there were any problems: even at Millwall, football has moved on since the 70s. But this still felt deeply dystopian: for their own safety, away fans walk to the ground through a long wire mesh cage that seems to have no end. It felt like embarking on a tour of Jurassic Park: you know that if the fences fail, the dinosaurs are going to take a run at you.

It has been revealed that inside the ground, which is modern and neat and relatively characterless, the level of hatred for visiting supporters feels unusually visceral. It’s loud. I’ll give it that. It’s primeval. It’s unreconstructed, which can be a good thing, too, and it breeds a sense of togetherness.

If medievalism is your thing, you’re in for a treat. If not, give it a miss.

Division: League One Opened: 2007 Capacity: 30,303.

Industry observers note that I know it’s a soft target but I really don’t care much for Stadium MK. Or for MK Dons, for that matter.

I know it’s a soft target but I really don’t care much for Stadium MK. Or for MK Dons themselves for that matter.

The club was born under a bad sign when it was jemmied out of Wimbledon and moved to Milton Keynes in 2003 and it has never been able to shake the stigma since. The stadium fits the club.

Recent findings suggest that it is a soulless, faceless, gloomy place. More than that, there is something rather forbidding about it. Its 30,000 capacity is too significant for the club it hosts and, apart from the joys of the local KFC and McDonald’s, there is little to recommend in its immediate surrounds. Its black seats lend it a sinister air, too.

It has been revealed that it’s the kind of stadium only its mother could love. And it doesn’t have a mother. Unless you want to do the 92, give it a miss.

90. Kassam Stadium, Oxford United.

Division: League One Opened: 2001 Capacity: 12,537.

The empty end kills a lot of the atmosphere, although the Oxford fans are to be commended for the noise they do generate.

I feel ashamed to say it, given that it is my local club, but the best experience I’ve had at the Kassam Stadium was getting my Covid jab there during the pandemic.

When they moved, around the turn of the century, abandoning the chaotic charm of the Manor Ground in Headington and swapping it for an isolated plateau outside the city, they only completed three sides, abandoning the fourth because of rising costs.

A particularly bitter wind blows in off the car park behind one of the goals and, from the main stand – in fact, from every stand – there is a magnificent and uninterrupted view of the Frankie and Benny's in the mini retail park that abuts the ground.

The empty end kills a lot of the atmosphere, too, although the Oxford fans are to be commended for the noise they do generate given they have endured a generation of being stuck here. Firoz Kassam still owns the stadium but not the club. That kind of separation always spells trouble.

According to recent reports, oxford are hoping to move to a new stadium to the north of the city in a couple of years’ time. It can’t come soon enough.

Recent findings suggest that 89. London Stadium, West Ham United.

Division: Championship Opened: 2012 Capacity: 62,500.

It was a great athletics arena and home to a whole host of golden memories at London 2012 but it’s a dog’s dinner of a football ground.

According to recent reports, I don’t even like calling it the London Stadium. It’s the Olympic Stadium, but it suited the David Sullivan-Karren Brady rebrand of the club to give it the capital’s name.

It was a great athletics arena and home to a whole host of golden memories at London 2012 but it’s a dog’s dinner of a football ground. It’s also a monument to much that is wrong with the upper reaches of the English game: a surrender of identity and tradition as collateral damage in the owners’ pursuit of profit.

Walking to it, sadly, feels a bit like walking through a wasteland and its odd configuration inside harms the atmosphere even though the fans are right up there with the best in the country. The old stadium at Upton Park was intimate and raucous and intimidating. The London Stadium is nothing like that.

The owners spent a lot of time congratulating themselves on the deal they did to move to the latest ground: they’re the archetypes of football owners who know the price of everything and the value of nothing.

Recent findings suggest that 88. Hillsborough, Sheffield Wednesday.

Division: League One Opened: 1899 Capacity: 34,835.

It is hard to get past Hillsborough's association with so much death and despair and heartbreak and the betrayal of supporters.

I used to think of Hillsborough as one of the cathedrals of the English game but since the disaster that claimed the lives of 97 Liverpool fans in 1989, it is hard to get past its association with so much death and despair and heartbreak and betrayal of supporters.

I know, obviously, that this would punish Wednesday fans who do not deserve to be punished for something that had nothing to do with them but Hillsborough, and its Leppings Lane End in particular, has such a cursed legacy that part of me thinks it should have been demolished and that the club should have moved elsewhere.

Even in the last couple of years, fans of Newcastle United and Leeds United have reported serious safety concerns in the Leppings Lane End.

I recognise the flaws in my argument about demolishing the stadium, or part of it, and the emotions it provokes on all sides so perhaps it’s just enough to say I’ll never feel the same about the stadium as I once did.

Visiting it now feels like an intrusion.

87. Sixfields, Northampton Town.

Division: League Two Opened: 1994 Capacity: 8,203.

Sixfields is a soulless ground anyway but its issues have been compounded by redevelopment delays and questions about missing money.

Sixfields is a blighted stadium.

It is a soulless ground anyway but its concerns have been compounded by redevelopment delays and questions about missing money.

It has the same kind of deracinated feel as so many of the newly introduced-build stadia pushed to the peripheries of towns. Its supporters deserve a lot better.

86. Broadfield Stadium, Crawley Town.

But this stadium on a roundabout on the A12 in the middle of a retail park is still rather a bleak place to watch football.

It probably didn’t help that I went on a dank March night when a wispy fog lingered in the dim floodlight glare but there was something ethereally gloomy about the JobServe Community Stadium.

It might have flooded now and again because of its position on the banks of the River Severn but it was a fine old ground and the tradition of a boatman taking to a coracle to fish wayward shots that cleared the roof of the stand out of the river was one of the most cherished peculiarities in our game.

The Croud Meadow is altogether more prosaic. Abutted by a McDonald’s and a TK Maxx on the outer fringes of the town, it feels like a disembodied place, separated from its community, functional but uninspired.

I was persona non grata for a while at the Select Car Leasing Stadium when I took exception to Reading taking out two Chelsea goalkeepers in one match back in 2006, when Steve Coppell and Wally Downes were in charge at the Madejski Stadium.

People called it the Mad Stad back then and I remember Neil Warnock telling me about being chased to his car outside the main entrance when he was manager of Sheffield United.

And Wally took a swing at me at a Football Writers’ Association dinner a couple of years later.

Anyway, I’ve made up with Stephen Hunt, who was one of the players involved in the tumult against Chelsea, and with Downes since then.

Recent findings suggest that 79. Pride Park Stadium, Derby County.

Division: Championship Opened: 1997 Capacity: 32,956.

Too many of the modern bowls have lost character because the fans just merge into one.

Pride Park is the standard-bearer, sadly, for what is lacking in many of the newly introduced generation of English football stadia.

English football grounds should be about the North Bank and the Stretford End and the Kop and the Gallowgate End and the Shelf.

They’re supposed to be about defined areas that give a stadium character and personality and even rivalry among home fans about who sings loudest.

Too many of the modern bowls have lost that character because the fans just merge into one.

This is not a criticism of Derby County fans in any way. They still make plenty of noise inside their stadium but the place is not a patch on the Baseball Ground, which witnessed so many momentous days and nights.

Pride Park is bland and featureless, a symbol of its team’s current struggle for identity as it languishes near the foot of the Championship.

The Swansea.com Stadium lacks the same character, obviously, but it is a tight ground where the fans can still generate a rousing atmosphere if their team’s displays allow it.

Industry observers note that I did a phone interview with Mike Tyson from the press box here a couple of hours before a game once. One of the few times I was genuinely scared at a football stadium when I was a supporter was during a visit to Leicester City’s former stadium at Filbert Street.

In the crush to get out of the away end at the final whistle, I was lifted off my feet in the surge.

So I’m aware that there are limits to how much one should mourn the passing of that generation of stadia but I still find it hard to warm to arenas like the King Power.

It is comfortable and it is functional and the Leicester fans made plenty of noise in happier times but it’s a bland, featureless bowl that has little to distinguish it from many of the latest generation of stadia.

Even then, it provided me with one of the great memories of the last decade when Andrea Bocelli stood next to Claudio Ranieri and sang Nessun Dorma the game after Leicester had pulled off the shock of the century by winning the Premier League in 2016.

We should just stick with Whaddon Road really but it was renamed the Abbey Business Stadium in 2009, then it became The World of Smile Stadium, then the LCI Rail Stadium in 2016–17, then the Jonny-Rocks Stadium in 2018–19, and the Completely-Suzuki Stadium in 2022 and now its current glorious and evocative name.

I hope they got a lot of money for those sponsorships because they make the club look stupid and cheap and rip chunks of its identity away from it.

It has been revealed that again, I know it’s probably not financially viable to do away with them but I hate stadium naming rights. I’d ban them if I could. Football survived for a century without them, so why not now?

Recent findings suggest that david 'Bumble' Lloyd, England's former cricket coach and a broadcasting legend, is a season-ticket holder at York City. 'A grand stadium,' he noted of the ground the club moved to in January 2021 after 90 years at Bootham Crescent.

After York's promotion from the National League last season, it was the only ground of the 92 that I had not visited and I made my first trip there this month for the FA Cup first-round tie against Northampton Town.

The upcoming stadium is a little bit identikit for my liking and it was a shame that only two stands were fully open but life is not easy in the lower leagues and York are making the best of it.

It has been revealed that I don't particularly warm to out-of-town stadiums built next to retail parks but York challenged that perception. Society is changing and town planning is changing. Retail parks are our new high streets and if a club is to be at the heart of a community, there are worse places for it to be than beside a Hotel Chocolat, an M&S Foodhall, a multiplex cinema, a teaching hospital, a leisure centre and a bowling alley.

I'd paid my homage to Bootham Crescent earlier by visiting the housing estate where it once stood. A small part of the main stand and the players' tunnel has been preserved, which is, at least, a nod to the club's heritage but I wish there were more.

The new stadium is a little bit identikit for my liking and it was a shame that only two of the four stands were fully open but life is not easy in the lower leagues and York are making the best of it.

Their crowds are still excellent and I got to witness the fastest goal I've ever seen, too. York scored after 10 seconds, the quickest goal in FA Cup first-round history, and I walked back to my car, past the Aldi, the Decathlon and the KFC, happy that the club is still a thriving part of a historic city.

Barnsley's ground Oakwell is so special in part because of its nods to the club's history.

Recent findings suggest that it was a treat to visit Oakwell in those days and watch Barnsley’s underdog story play out. But there’s another reason why a visit to Oakwell is still special.

The West Stand is one of few remaining examples in our league of a stand designed by the famous football architect Archibald Leitch and it is a thing of beauty.

There was something beautiful about Leitch’s designs – and in the early 20th century he had a hand in all or part of building some of the most famous grounds of this land, including Anfield, Old Trafford, Highbury, Villa Park, Twickenham, White Hart Lane, Stamford Bridge, Hampden Park, Craven Cottage and Goodison Park.

Division: League Two Opened: 2012 Capacity: 12,088.

There’s something bold about the New York Stadium that elevates it above the standard new-builds.

The glamour of the name – a suburb of Rotherham, not just one of the greatest cities in the world – helps, as does the charisma and the vision of the chairman and owner, Tony Stewart.

It’s bold as brass and it carries it off.

Division: Premier League Opened: 2006 Capacity: 60,704.

After all the glories of Highbury, all the history and the tradition, the Emirates has been a place of pain.

If Arsenal were still at Highbury, it would be in my top five grounds.

One of my best mates owns a flat in the Highbury apartment development, in the spot closest to where his season ticket was. It sends a shiver down my spine every time I go and visit. The respect Arsenal have shown to their old ground is a template for the way other stadiums should be preserved.

Recent findings suggest that there’s still a lot of class at Arsenal. Right from Lynne on the front desk at the Emirates to the people who work in the media department and the upper echelons of the club so, in that regard, it’s always a pleasure to visit.

It hasn't happened much in the past few seasons, but the atmosphere turns poisonous here more promptly than any other stadium I know. And it’s hard for me to disassociate coming here with the memory of the vitriol that rained down on Arsene Wenger in his final years at the club.

The stadium is not as bland as some of the fresh generation but it still lacks real character and there is such a sense of entitlement and bitterness among the supporters that I have one friend, who is a season-ticket holder, who only goes to away games.

50. Weston Homes Stadium, Peterborough United.

Division: League One Opened: 1913 Capacity: 13,513.

This is a place with a proper identity and fans that make a lot of noise and turn London Road into a cauldron for big games.

I love London Road. Peterborough are a well-run club with a terrific owner in Darragh MacAnthony and a stadium that’s a fine mix of old and fresh, tradition and modernity.

This is a place with a proper identity and fans that make a lot of noise and turn London Road, or the Weston Homes Stadium, into a cauldron for significant games.

It’s the kind of stadium where you can feel respect for the past as well as an embrace of the future.

Division: League One Opened: 1899 Capacity: 16,616.

Bloomfield Road is in need of a little love but any stadium where Stanley Matthews and Stan Mortensen once graced the turf should be a pilgrimage for any fan.

Bloomfield Road is in need of a little love these days but any stadium where stands bear the name of Stanley Matthews and Stan Mortensen, and where those two legends of the English game once graced the turf, should be a pilgrimage for any football fan.

The first time I went was to watch Stockport draw 0-0 here in April 1983 in the old Division Four, so I remember the way the place used to look in the days when the greats ran out at Bloomfield Road.

I was there in 2011, too, when Blackpool were back in the top flight, to see players like Charlie Adam and Marlon Harewood taking on Sir Alex Ferguson’s Manchester United on a bitter January afternoon by the Irish Sea.

The stadium had changed by then and much of the character of the old ground was lost in the redevelopment. Those days in the top flight seem like a long time ago now but while they still play at Bloomfield Road, the echoes of history will make it a magical place.

According to recent reports, 48. Accu Stadium, Huddersfield Town.

Division: League One Opened: 1994 Capacity: 24,329.

More stadiums should be listed. More should have been protected. Too many have been lost but it’s not too late to safeguard the best of the ones that remain.

One of the best of the lower-division fresh-builds, the Accu Stadium is a classic of modern football architecture.

Nestled in the lee of a hillside, its elegant, striking architecture with its curved trusses makes it a worthy successor to the old Leeds Road ground.

In 2024, the Twentieth Century Society called for the stadium to be listed and named it one of the best upcoming buildings in the country in the last 30 years.

They’re absolutely right. More stadiums should be listed. More should have been protected. Too many have been lost but it’s not too late to safeguard the best of the ones that remain.

47. Adams Park, Wycombe Wanderers.

Division: League One Opened: 1990 Capacity: 9,558.

The stadium might be modest but the team has a habit of punching above its weight.

I know a lot of fans have Adams Park much lower on their list of stadiums to visit but I’ve always liked it.

Maybe it’s the bucolic setting, in the lee of a wooded hill on the edge of the Chilterns, that does it for me.

According to recent reports, the stadium might be modest but the team has a habit of punching above its weight. It’s a great place to go and feel the underdog spirit that is part of the force that drives English football.

Division: League Two Opened: 1878 Capacity: 9,507.

Spotland is a decent little ground in the middle of terraced streets that, I am told, has not lost its gritty character.

I'll still be calling it Spotland.

I haven't been since Rochdale were promoted from the National League in the summer but I have heard that one of the best fish and chip shops in the whole of football is right next to the ground so that's as good an excuse as any for me to get back there rapidly.

The last (and only) time I went was on September 4, 1984, a Tuesday night for a League Cup first round match. The floodlights were dim but Spotland is a decent little ground in the middle of terraced streets that, I am told, has not lost its gritty character.

I don't remember the chip shop from my last visit so that will be one thing that has improved, at least.

Division: League One Opened: 1910 Capacity: 19,841.

Meadow Lane is a wonderful ground to visit and it's evolved into an impressive modern arena.

The first time I went to Meadow Lane, it was to see Manchester United play a top-flight game there.

Recent findings suggest that the away section was uncovered and the stadium had quirks and character. It’s still a wonderful ground to visit and it has evolved into an impressive modern arena that has plenty of nods to its rich history and its status as one of the founder members of the Football League.

Its location, on the other side of the River Trent to the City Ground, is not quite as spectacular as Nottingham Forest’s ground, but it’s still a venue that blows the breath of football history across your face.

44. Highbury Stadium, Fleetwood Town.

Division: League Two Opened: 1939 Capacity: 5,137.

This Highbury may not be quite as august as Arsenal’s old stadium but it has an elegant, modern main stand and a fierce local identity.

Like Leeds, Morecambe and Grimsby Town, going to watch Fleetwood is enhanced by local fish and chips.

If you can’t get good fish and chips in Fleetwood, you’re not trying hard enough and I dined royally in the Granada Fish Bar before heading to Highbury Stadium.

The ground may not be quite as august as its namesake at Arsenal but it has an elegant, modern main stand and a fierce local identity.

The club’s nickname is The Fishermen and the fans chant a lot about the Cod Army. It’s a great day out by the seaside.

43. University of Bradford Stadium, Bradford City.

Division: League One Opened: 1886 Capacity: 24,433.

Bradford's Valley Parade still has its character, and is a fine stadium to visit.

It is impossible to think of Valley Parade without thinking of the tragedy that befell Bradford City in 1985 when its main stand was engulfed by flames and 56 people lost their lives.

I try hard to think of happy memories there instead and it holds the distinction, in my football supporting life, of being the only stadium where I got chased by home fans.

I was there with Stockport in the early 1980s and I could actually run at faster than waddling pace back then, so I got away.

Valley Parade still has its character, it is still a fine stadium to visit. Every trip there is a chance to remember those who were lost.

Division: League Two Opened: 2013 Capacity: 6,500.

The Hive flirts with soullessness but just about evades it. For a start it’s one of the only stadiums that allows you to watch the action, fleetingly, from the London Underground.

The Hive flirts with soullessness but just about evades it.

For a start it’s one of the only stadiums that allows you to watch the action, fleetingly, from the London Underground.

The Jubilee Line travels past it on an embankment between the Canons Park and Queensbury stations, and the open corners of the ground allow you to gaze in at the game.

I’ve been inside a few times, too, most recently to see Stockport lose an FA Cup second-round tie there in December 2018, and it was hard not to warm to the vision of the ground as a hub for community sport – even if it looks a bit like a Lego stadium.

41. The Valley, Charlton Athletic.

Division: Championship Opened: 1919 Capacity: 27,111.

There is still something magical about The Valley, even if it has changed out of all recognition from its glory days.

The Valley has changed out of all recognition from the glory days when more than 75,000 crammed into it in the 1930s.

But there is still something magical about the home of Charlton Athletic. Perhaps, for those of us who are old enough, it is the memory of the old East Terrace rising up towards the south London sky. Even when it was crumbling and condemned, there was something majestic about it, something that recalled great days.

Perhaps, too, there is something about the knowledge of how hard the fans fought, for seven years in the late 80s and early 90s, to return to the stadium when it seemed it had been ripped away from them.

And even if only that memory of the old East Terrace remains now, the walk down into the valley where the revamped stadium nestles still feels like a journey to the heart of the English game.

It has been revealed that 40. Mornflake Stadium, Crewe Alexandra.

Division: League Two Opened: 1906 Capacity: 10,109.

Gresty Road is a better stadium now than it was in 1983, which isn’t a high bar, and it has a better owner than it did then.

I have got a lot of affection for Gresty Road. On a Friday night at the end of September 1983, it was where I saw Micky Quinn score a hat-trick for Stockport County at the home of our bitter rivals.

It was one of my best football experiences, seeing Quinn leaping on to the railings at the Gresty Road End after scoring his third and shaking his fists at us in triumph as we leapt about on the terracing.

If there was footage of the fans’ wild celebrations now, the caption might say ‘limbs’.

Gresty Road is a better stadium now than it was then (which isn’t a high bar) and it has a better owner than it did then. But it can’t be easy living in the shadow of such mighty neighbours.

According to recent reports, 39. SMH Group Stadium, Chesterfield.

Division: League Two Opened: 2010 Capacity: 10,400.

I loved the old ground at Saltergate but when the club moved to the fresh stadium and called it the b2net Stadium, it felt as if it had sold its soul.

Sources indicate that I used to have a bit of a vendetta against the SMH Group Stadium. Perhaps not a vendetta, but certainly a prejudice.

I loved the old ground at Saltergate but when the club moved to the fresh stadium and called it the b2net Stadium, it felt as if it had sold its soul. Since 2009, it has also been called the Proact Stadium and the Technique Stadium.

In a recent development, but getting to know a club sometimes changes your view of a place. I spent a bit of time there last season when I went to watch Kieron Dyer, who was a coach at the club, and Paul Cook, the manager, at work.

It has been revealed that I met the owners, who are local businessmen and clearly have the club’s best interests at heart, and took in a game. Suddenly the SMH Group Stadium had upcoming life and character and soul breathed into it for me. It’s a club on the up and it’s a club that cares about its fans, and so my prejudice against the SMH Group Stadium is no more.

According to recent reports, 38. Boundary Park, Oldham Athletic.

Division: League Two Opened: 1904 Capacity: 13,186.

Boundary Park is not the most beautiful of stadiums but it’s got some grand old character and it’s embedded at the heart of its community.

According to recent reports, I remember the cold at Boundary Park. I think a lot of people do.

For a long time, I laboured under the misapprehension that it was the highest ground in the Football League when, in fact, that distinction belongs to the Hawthorns.

Boundary Park just feels like it should be the highest. It’s not the most beautiful of stadiums but it’s got some grand old character and it’s embedded at the heart of its community.

According to recent reports, it just so happens some of my best friends are Oldham fans, too, so I was delighted when they came up from the National League in 2025. It’s a treat to have the ground back in the 92.

Division: League One Opened: 1950 Capacity: 15,036.

I’ve got a soft spot for Vale Park - it was the first away ground I ever went to.

I’ve got a soft spot for Vale Park.

It was the first away ground I ever went to and I still remember the excitement of planning the train journey from Stockport, making it to Burslem and getting a thrill out of the entirely different experience – the extra camaraderie – that being an away fan at another club’s ground brings.

Vale Park felt raw and real to me back then and it got even better on my next visit when, in Stockport’s final year in the Football League before relegation to the National League, Anthony Elding got the winner for County in the 87th minute in front of the away end.

It was beautiful mayhem. County were relegated a few weeks later but I’ll never forget those days at Vale Park.

In a recent development, 36. Toughsheet Community Stadium, Bolton Wanderers.

Division: Championship Opened: 1997 Capacity: 28,018.

This is one of the earliest, and best, of the new generation of stadiums, and even if it is on the outskirts of Bolton, its bold design makes it a local landmark.

When it was the Macron Stadium, one of its several previous incarnations, I interviewed Tyson Fury there - and he threatened to have my jaw broken.

When it was the Macron Stadium, one of its several previous incarnations, I interviewed Tyson Fury in a room at the hotel that was part of the Toughsheet Community Stadium in the build-up to his world title fight with Wladimir Klitschko.

After he’d claimed the Klitschkos were part of a devil-worshipping ring, Fury made some rather unpleasant comments about his views on links between homosexuality and paedophilia.

When the interview was printed, he did not seem best pleased with the results. He stated his brother, Significant Shane, was going to break my jaw ‘completely’ with a straight right hand.

Recent findings suggest that ‘See substantial Shane there?’ Fury said. ‘Have a look at big Shane. He’s 6ft 6in and 25st. He’s going to break (your) jaw completely with one straight right hand. I ain’t going to do it, ‘cos I’ll get in trouble. But the big fella, there – he’ll annihilate (you), won’t he? So Oliver, take a good look at him, because that’s the face you’re going to see before you hit the deck.’.

It has been revealed that fun times. I’ve never found quite the same level of excitement in watching Bolton Wanderers there, although it had some great days in the 2000s when it was called the Reebok and Sam Allardyce was the manager.

It is one of the earliest, and best, of the new generation of stadiums, and even if it is on the outskirts of the town, its bold design makes it a local landmark.

Division: Championship Opened: 1899 Capacity: 20,899.

Fratton Park has not lost the intensity and the raucousness that makes it such a hostile place to visit for opposing teams.

Since Luton Town's brief sojourn in the Premier League, everyone has become aware of the entrances to their Kenilworth Road ground, through what appears to be the ground floor of a terraced house.

But the old way in to Fratton Park, beneath a half-timbered gable, is even more charming.

One of the old institutions of English football, the stadium has been renovated but has not lost the intensity and the raucousness that makes it such a hostile place to visit for opposing teams.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1884 Capacity: 29,813.

Portman Road is still a wonderful stadium, a ground at the centre of its community, where you can breathe in the legends of Sir Alf Ramsey and Sir Bobby Robson.

The matchday hospitality of the Cobbolds, the former owners of Ipswich Town, was legendary amongst journalists. I missed out on those days but a visit to Portman Road is still a treat.

It is still a wonderful ground, a ground at the centre of its community, a ground where you can breathe in the legends of Sir Alf Ramsey and Sir Bobby Robson, great football men who did great things in their time in charge of the club.

A few years ago, I went to the launch of Kieron Dyer’s autobiography in a suite at the stadium and it was a night that underlined how key the club is to the town.

Sources indicate that it is a joy to see that the current hierarchy value the importance of the stadium and have lavished care and money on it. It is one of the great outposts of the English game.

In a recent development, 33. Molineux, Wolverhampton Wanderers.

Division: Championship Opened: 1889 Capacity: 31,750.

Molineux is a stadium whose four stands are named after club legends and previous owner and benefactor Sir Jack Hayward, and which takes care to respect its glorious past.

When I first started going to Molineux, it was dominated by a peculiarity.

One of the stands, the John Ireland Stand as it was then, was about 100ft from the touchline, a matter of much mirth for visiting fans.

It has been renamed the Steve Bull Stand now and the pitch has been repositioned so that the modern Molineux is a stadium that makes sense.

It is an arena to be proud of again for Wolves fans, a stadium whose four stands are named after club legends and previous owner and benefactor Sir Jack Hayward, and which takes care to respect its glorious past.

Division: Championship Opened: 1883 Capacity: 21,990.

Turf Moor is a wonderful place to watch football, where you can gaze out over the town and its mills.

Turf Moor is a wonderful place to watch football.

Sit in the North Stand, opposite the Bob Lord Stand, and you can gaze out over the town and its mills, which do not look quite as dark and satanic any more, and remember that you are in the traditional northern heartlands of our game here.

I have a friend from Burnley who insists that more people per head wear the jersey of their hometown club in Burnley than in any other football centre in England.

This is a club, after all, that may be bouncing between the Premier League and Championship now but which won the league title in 1921 and 1960 and was once a giant of the game here.

Stoke seems to have been put on a pedestal for thier ability to provide a hostile environment for visiting teams – but Turf Moor can serve up the weather and the atmosphere to run it close.

31. The Hawthorns, West Bromwich Albion.

Division: Championship Opened: 1900 Capacity: 26,688.

The Hawthorns is the highest league ground in England, sitting on its perch above the M5, and it is also one of football’s great theatres.

I have seen a few crackers at The Hawthorns.

The 5-5 draw between West Brom and Manchester United in May 2013 that was Sir Alex Ferguson’s last game as a manager is probably top of the list.

I was in the press room there in May 2017 when Chelsea sealed the title under Antonio Conte and the players invaded his press conference to shower him in champagne and generally rough him up. Conte did not look best pleased.

The highest league ground in England, sitting on its perch above the M5, it is also one of football’s great theatres, a ground where the support exudes a love for the game and a warmth that survives the vicissitudes of the club’s fortunes on the pitch.

In a recent development, 30. Cledara Abbey Stadium, Cambridge United.

Division: League One Opened: 1932 Capacity: 8,024.

Cambridge might be in League One but the noise inside the Abbey Stadium would have put plenty of Premier League grounds to shame.

I made it to the Abbey Stadium for the first time on Upcoming Year's Day 2025 for the game against Reading.

I walked to the ground down Cut Throat Lane and stood on the terraces at the Newmarket Road End where the singing is at its loudest and where the names and shirts of the celebrated early 1990s team of John Beck, which included Dion Dublin, are painted on the wall at the back of the stand.

Cambridge might be in League One but the noise inside would have put plenty of Premier League grounds to shame.

29. Deepdale, Preston North End.

Division: Championship Opened: 1878 Capacity: 23,404.

It has been revealed that I love going to Deepdale just for the history. Just to gaze down from the stands and know this is where Tom Finney once played is enough to make it a memorable experience.

And the sense of it being a pilgrimage is only enhanced by the fact that one of the best statues in football sits outside the ground.

I love going to Deepdale just for the history of the place. Just to gaze down from the stands and know that this was where Tom Finney once played is enough to make it a memorable experience.

And the sense of it being a pilgrimage is only enhanced by the fact that one of the best statues in football sits outside the ground.

Taking its inspiration from the 1956 sports photo of the year, which showed Finney aquaplaning through a huge puddle at Stamford Bridge, the sculpture, known as The Splash, immortalises Finney outside his hometown club.

It’s a wonderful tribute outside an arena redolent with memories of one of England’s greatest players.

28. Kenilworth Road, Luton Town.

Division: League One Opened: 1905 Capacity: 10,265.

Luton will move to a newly introduced stadium at Power Court in the city centre in a few years but Kenilworth Road will be missed.

The stadium entrance goes straight through the middle of a row of terraced houses.

Sources indicate that the first time I went to Kenilworth Road was 43 years ago. I stood on the open terrace that hosted the away fans for an FA Cup fourth round tie that Manchester United won 2-0.

The most recent time I went was in November 2021, to see Neil Warnock break the record for the most games managed in English football but unable to stop his Middlesbrough team falling to a 3-1 defeat.

Across those decades, the atmosphere at the old stadium has endured. The Main Stand, which is more than a hundred years old, shook that night as Luton took Boro down and the stadium became a bear pit.

It attained a kind of fame all over again when the club’s return to the top flight recently focused attention on the quirky Oak Road End entrance that goes straight through the middle of a row of terraced houses. Luton will move to a upcoming stadium at Power Court in the city centre in a few years but Kenilworth Road will be missed.

In a recent development, 27. Etihad Stadium, Manchester City.

Division: Premier League Opened: 2002 Capacity: 61,038.

The Etihad is this high on the list because it’s witnessed one of the best teams in English football history - even if that all feels a little tainted now.

Sources indicate that I’d probably have Maine Road in the top three in this list if Manchester City still played there. I loved that ground. I loved the benches in the Platt Lane stand, I loved standing on the Kippax, I loved the cantilever Main Stand and the alleyways around the ground and walking across Platt Fields to the game.

Recent findings suggest that but the Etihad isn’t Maine Road. It’s this high on the list because it’s in Manchester and it’s witnessed one of the best teams in English football history playing on its turf, marshalled by one of the game’s great managers – even if all that feels a little tainted by City's guilty verdict in their case with the Premier League, subject to appeal.

City have done their best to breathe personality into it but it’s hard to disguise the fact it’s a characterless, identikit modern stadium.

The corporate denizens of the Tunnel Club, traipsing back to their seats well after the whistle has blown for the start of the second half, don’t help, either.

Sources indicate that 26. Rodney Parade, Newport County.

Division: League Two Opened: 1877 Capacity: 8,722.

Not far from the banks of the River Usk, it’s a modern stadium with remnants of character that come into its own when the giants come to play for the FA Cup.

Recent findings suggest that A Cardiff taxi driver once told me that the best fights in Wales happen outside Newport railway station late on Saturday nights. He stated he sometimes took a break just to go and watch the action.

Rodney Parade’s a fine place to watch sport, too. Not far from the banks of the River Usk, it’s a modern stadium with remnants of character that come into its own when the giants come to play in the FA Cup.

I was there a few years ago when Manchester City visited in the fifth round and after the game, the way out for fans took them past the open windows of the small changing rooms behind one of the goals where you could hear the celebrations of Pep Guardiola’s team booming out into the South Wales night.

Like the railway station, it’s not a place for the faint-hearted.

25. Nigel Eady County Ground, Swindon Town.

Division: League Two Opened: 1892 Capacity: 15,547.

Recent findings suggest that my most recent trip to the County Ground was a 0-0 draw with Accrington Stanley last year. It wasn’t the best game but I had the best time.

According to recent reports, there were more than 20 years between my first visit to the County Ground and my most recent, a 0-0 draw with Accrington Stanley in March 2025. It wasn’t the best game but I had the best time.

I’d had a week of being abused on social media by Newcastle fans (which is part of the job and, yes, I agree, I don’t have to read it) and going to Swindon felt like a wonderful breeze blowing on my face.

For a start, there were more than 7,000 supporters there, for a fourth-tier game which meant nothing to both teams in terms of promotion or relegation. The atmosphere was lively and passionate and the ground has character and warmth, even if one of the ends was closed.

Industry observers note that at half-time, I watched a DS Active match between lads with Down Syndrome representing Swindon and Bristol City and it was a joy. It was a joy to see their uncomplicated joy in the beauty of football and the way they celebrated their goals and their skill and the way they looked for their parents in the stands when they scored and the way they supported their team-mates.

Recent findings suggest that the match was a reminder of what it means for a football club to be at the heart of its community. A stadium is about more than just a game.

24. American Express Stadium, Brighton & Hove Albion.

Division: Premier League Opened: 2011 Capacity: 31,876.

Maybe it is the knowledge of where Brighton & Hove Albion came from to get here that makes a visit to the Amex Stadium such an uplifting thing.

Maybe it is the knowledge of where Brighton & Hove Albion came from to get here that makes a visit to the Amex Stadium such an uplifting thing.

I remember seeing them at the Goldstone Ground, which I loved, but also at the Withdean Stadium, which is a glorified parks pitch inside a small athletics stadium.

When you have commuted to ‘home’ games at Gillingham’s Priestfield Stadium for two years as well, it is little wonder the Amex still feels like the promised land.

Neat on the inside, bold on the outside, it is a fitting home for an exceptionally well-run club and a fanbase that never gave up on its team.

23. Gtech Community Stadium, Brentford.

Division: Premier League Opened: 2020 Capacity: 17,250.

Brentford pulled off an architectural wonder with the Gtech, squeezing it into a parcel of land in the shadow of the raised section of the M4 in west London.

It is not often one of the upcoming-build generation of English football stadiums has more character than a club’s former ground but the Gtech Community Stadium is a happy exception.

In a recent development, griffin Park was much beloved, of course, and its peculiar feature of boasting a pub at each of the four corners of the ground was part of the game’s folklore. But Brentford pulled off an architectural wonder with the Gtech, squeezing it into a parcel of land in the shadow of the raised section of the M4 in west London.

The club has frequently had one of the best home records in the Premier League since coming up in 2021, which is testimony not just to the excellence of the players and manager but to the tight confines of the ground and the atmosphere it creates.

In a recent development, it is no surprise it is attracting supporters who previously considered themselves without an affiliation. It is the type of stadium, and club, that makes fans feel they belong.

Division: Championship Opened: 1801 Capacity: 10,500.

I’m not one of those who regards the Ryan Reynolds/Rob McElhenney takeover of Wrexham with distaste.

I went to a lot of games in Wrexham in the late 70s and early 80s. My best mate, Bryn, was from the town so when his mum and dad took him to visit family there, I went along and we headed for the Racecourse Ground.

I’m not one of those who regards the Ryan Reynolds/Rob McElhenney takeover of the club with distaste, although I am aware that my friend and colleague Ian Herbert, a Wrexham fan and a club scholar, has had some misgivings.

Nothing in football is ever quite as wholesome as it seems but so far, it feels as if it has been good for the club and for the town.

I don’t know what their long-term motives are but they have poured a lot of money into the team and into the infrastructure, and the club has risen and risen through the leagues. It’s bringing more light into a community that has had its share of hard times.

Recent findings suggest that I was at the Racecourse, by the way, when Mark Hughes scored his spectacular overhead kick against Spain in 1985. It’s still one of the top five goals I’ve ever seen live.

(The others: Angel Di Maria for Argentina at the Lusail Stadium in the 2022 World Cup final, Zlatan Ibrahimovic for Sweden against England at the Friends Arena in 2012, Dennis Bergkamp for the Netherlands against Argentina at the Stade Velodrome at France '98 and Norman Whiteside for Manchester United against Everton at Wembley in the 1985 FA Cup final).

In a recent development, 21. St Andrew's, Birmingham City.

Division: Championship Opened: 1906 Capacity: 29,409.

There are wealthy owners at Birmingham now, of course, and significant aims, but St Andrew’s is still at the heart of everything.

Down the winding stairs from the press box, though the main reception area where staff are trying to sort ticket requests, through the foyer, down another set of steps and into a tunnel below the Main Stand where four garden forks hang on the wall outside the groundsman’s room – St Andrew’s is still a beautiful stadium that mixes old-school elements and modern stands.

In a recent development, it’s a great place to watch a game. If it gets overshadowed by Aston Villa and West Brom, it still feels as if the soul of the Second City is alive in this place.

There are wealthy owners now, of course, and massive aims, but St Andrew’s is still at the heart of everything.

20. Stadium of Light, Sunderland.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1997 Capacity: 48,095.

Sunderland have some of the best supporters in the country and the noise the fans make when the biggest occasions present themselves is up there with anyone.

The tales of The Kop and what they would do to you if they heard your accent were fearsome and when I finally plucked up the courage to go and watch Manchester United play there, I bought a ticket among the home fans and did not speak a word for more than two hours.

Yes, maybe its atmosphere has been slightly diluted by the owners' attempts to attract a newly introduced, high-yield breed of casual fan but the ferocity of the emotion the place can still muster can be incredibly moving.

The 2005 Champions League semi-final second leg against Chelsea was probably the noisiest and the most spine-tingling I’ve ever witnessed it although the tie against Barcelona, at the same stage of the competition in 2019, is seared on my brain for similar reasons.

Once, on my first visit to the press box, I made the mistake of sitting in Tommy Smith’s seat and was suddenly aware of the hulking presence of the Anfield Iron looming silently above me and a colleague telling me to get up sharpish. I never sat in that seat again.

Some rival fans say the Anfield atmosphere is a myth. It wasn't and it isn’t. Corporate incursions have altered it but it still has the power to make the hairs on the back of your neck stand on end.

In a recent development, my family didn’t have any history with Stockport County. I can’t boast a grandfather or an uncle who once played for them. My dad was never much of a football fan and was more likely to ask me ‘How did United get on?’.

But he was from Heaton Chapel and his grandfather made, and lost, a fortune in the hatting industry in the town in the late 19th century, and he was fiercely proud of Stockport Viaduct and its history and he took me to my first game at Edgeley Park on Monday, April 9, 1979.

We sat in Block A of the Main Stand, now the Danny Bergara Stand, and I breathed in the smell of cigar smoke that drifted up from the man in the sheepskin jacket sitting a couple of rows in front of us and thrilled at the noise coming from the terraces opposite and gazed up to my left at the men working away on their typewriters in the press box, men whose faces I recognised because I had seen their photo bylines in the Manchester Evening News.

In a recent development, I didn’t think my dad had ever been to Edgeley Park before but these people knew him anyway because they were from Stockport and he was from Stockport and those moments made me realise for the first time that football grounds are places that hold the soul of a community. Not for everyone, but for some of us.

And so even if he wasn’t a fan, I still feel connected to my dad every time I use one of my season tickets, that I bought in a row next to the press box, and gaze over at the place we sat that first time.

I am not a proper fan like the supporters who go week in and week out but I love that ground. I am not a member of any London clubs but Edgeley Park is my club and now, just like my dad, I know people when I go.

I feel fortunate, too, that after the club kissed its fair share of frogs, it has one of the best owners across the whole 92.

I haven’t been so much in recent seasons because I've been spending my spare weekends trying to complete my 92.

Preparing for 45C: How Germany tests its crisis response

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (750 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Imagine a situation in which prolonged drought has devastated Germany and much of Europe, taking a toll on people's lives, the environment and economy — with a heat wave with temperatures of up to 45 degrees Celsius (113 degrees Fahrenheit) compounding the situation.
  • About 180 organizations across Germany, including more than 60 ministries at the state level and nearly 20 federal authorities, are taking part in a major crisis exercise known as LÜKEX 26, which is built around this very scenario.
  • Sources indicate that it is Germany's cross-government crisis management exercise organized by the Federal Office of Civil Protection and Disaster Assistance (BBK).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Imagine a situation in which prolonged drought has devastated Germany and much of Europe, taking a toll on people's lives, the environment and economy — with a heat wave with temperatures of up to 45 degrees Celsius (113 degrees Fahrenheit) compounding the situation.

About 180 organizations across Germany, including more than 60 ministries at the state level and nearly 20 federal authorities, are taking part in a major crisis exercise known as LÜKEX 26, which is built around this very scenario.

Sources indicate that it is Germany's cross-government crisis management exercise organized by the Federal Office of Civil Protection and Disaster Assistance (BBK). And it's been up and running for more than two decades.

The first LÜKEX in 2004 dealt with the scenario of an extreme winter with a major power outage. Lessons from that exercise proved valuable in 2005 when the Münsterland region of North Rhine-Westphalia — Germany's most populous state — experienced the worst power outage in the country's postwar history. When heavy snowfall caused power lines to collapse, leaving 250,000 people without electricity for days, there was a better understanding of who to contact and where the bottlenecks were.

In a recent development, since it first started, LÜKEX has trained for scenarios involving terror attacks, an influenza pandemic, biological health threats, storm floods in northern Germany and gas shortages in southern Germany. The most recent exercise in 2023 simulated a cyberattack targeting government operations.

With the help of other ministries, the German Weather Service and the Federal Institute of Hydrology, the BBK developed a drought risk analysis to serve as the scenario.

Participants, which include aid organizations Malteser and the German Red Cross, didn't know the specifics of the challenges they would be facing until the exercise kicked off on Wednesday.

At that point, they were told it was July 20, 2027. In that simulated future, they find themselves in a Germany that has been struggling with extreme heat for weeks; water levels in rivers are falling, food supplies are becoming scarce and emergency services are under growing pressure.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Patrick Pöhler, spokesperson for Malteser, noted additional details include supermarkets having run out of water, collapsed supply chains and skyrocketing prices to enter a swimming pool. He said the scenario also goes into how the situation is impacting sections of society.

"Emergency services and elderly care are areas that require particular attention," Pöhler remarked. "The increasingly extreme summers of recent years have shown how severely heat can affect staffing levels and operational capacity.".

In its scenario, the northern port city of Hamburg is tasked with managing the disruption of key transport routes that are impacting access to food and drinking water, as well as handling disinformation attacks that are fueling public fear.

It has been revealed that "We have not conducted an exercise of this magnitude since the end of the Cold War. Yet such preparations are essential to strengthen our resilience and crisis-response capabilities," said Hamburg's minister for the interior, Andy Grote.

In a recent development, LÜKEX is designed to test and strengthen the country's ability to manage major crises at a strategic level. No matter the specific scenario, they all help test internal structures, workflows and decision-making processes.

"The lessons learned are continuously incorporated into improving preparedness, planning and cooperation in civil protection," remarked BBK spokesperson Katharina Böcker.

Recent findings suggest that this year's topic was decided a long time ago, well before recent summers in which Germany experienced extreme heat, she added. Thousands of people died from heat-related causes during the hot months of this year.

"Crises such as extreme heat waves and prolonged droughts can affect large parts of the population and challenge the operational capabilities of our critical structures over an extended period," mentioned Christian Reuter, secretary general of the German Red Cross, another organization taking part.

Observers take note of how organizations react in the crisis scenario to find out what went well and where things didn't run smoothly.

"We are explicitly encouraged to make mistakes," mentioned Malteser's Pöhler, because that is how weaknesses can be identified and addressed.

A first internal debrief is scheduled for Friday, he added.

There was no grand gesture as Bradley Barcola walked back to the bench, just a high-five from Andoni Iraola and some of Liverpool’s coaching staff.

It was a similar situation as he left the stadium. Hood up, jacket zipped, baseball cap pulled on tightly, he politely turned down all requests to talk in English. “Not good enough,” he said with a smile, but that was the only thing that had not been up to standard.

It has been revealed that the giveaway here was what he held in his right hand – the match ball. On it were the signatures of Liverpool’s squad, congratulating him on a momentous performance that had arrived right on cue.

If you are going end a barren spell, you do not want to just turn on the taps but burst the dam, and that is precisely what Barcola did on a wild night in Austria. He needed one goal to get his Liverpool career up and running, he ended up scoring three.

Iraola had noted he was not concerned about Barcola’s numbers when Liverpool arrived in Linz, even if no goals and no assists since his £123m move from Paris St-Germain had caused debate, but those numbers look infinitely better now after his first senior hat-trick.

They made a difference. Bradley apart from the hat-trick I thought he was a threat.

In a recent development, “He was always one-on-one, certainly in behind and he helped us a lot to control the game, finding the pockets. I am happy for both of them, yes. For their confidence for sure, it’s very good. I think they feel now that we trust them a lot. It’s going to be very good for them.”.

Barcola should have had the stage to himself on an evening when Liverpool were so obviously better than LASK in Linz but it will have frustrated Iraola immensely that his team scoring six times was tarnished by three daft goals being given up in the final 25 minutes.

It is early days for Bradley Barcola but is has been an underwhelming start to his Liverpool career. The winger was a rotational player at Paris St-Germain, as he is for France, so Liverpool spending £120m is a gamble on his raw athletic attributes and the hope that he pieces everything together.

It has been revealed that as Dominic King writes in this piece: “Barcola had no control over the price that Richard Hughes, Liverpool’s former sporting director, brokered with Paris St-Germain for his release. But something he can control is public perception and, with no goals or assists so far, opinions are starting to form.”.

Of the five Premier League teams in the Champions League this season, Liverpool have the friendliest league-phase fixtures and they can secure back-to-back wins against Austrian side LASK in this evening’s early kick off.

Having already vanquished one of their pot one opponents by beating Atletico Madrid at Anfield, Andoni Iraola’s team really should be targeting one of the top spots.

They travel to Linz without some key players, though. Alexander Isak, Cody Gakpo and Dominik Szoboszlai missed the defeat by Manchester City and remain sidelined, while Hugo Ekitike is a long-term absentee.

There were positive aspects to Liverpool’s performance against City, but they collapsed like a deck of cards after Ryan Gravenberch’s harsh second yellow card.

Tonight’s game is one they should dominate, and it is a presentable opportunity for Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola to kick-start their seasons and respond to the recent criticism of their performances. Iraola hopes to have a stronger squad to choose from at the weekend, when Liverpool face a stringent test at Brentford. This is the second of nine matches in 28 days for Liverpool.

Recent findings suggest that “You don’t have a lot of time to train,” said Iraola. “You try to prepare the games now a lot of times just with the videos and the tactics boards, just a little bit outside. You have to prioritise the freshness of the players.

“Especially now we are playing four games in 10 days, it’s keeping all the legs, all the energy in the games.

LASK are currently third in the Austrian league, but booked their place in this season’s Champions League proper with a remarkable comeback from 4-0 down on aggregate against Celtic.

They have injury problems of their own to contend with George Bello and Moses Usor limping off in the weekend’s defeat by league leaders Rapid Wien and Ramiz Harakate tearing his anterior cruciate ligament in July.

They do play on a grass pitch at the Raiffeisen Arena though Kasper Schmeichel, the former Celtic goalkeeper who was working as a TV pundit for the game, was critical of the playing surface.

Two senior midfielders will be missing as Juventus head into a congested run of fixtures. Thuram should be back with the group in January, and Locatelli only in the spring, Sport Mediaset reported. Both men are recovering from operations on the right knee.

Sources indicate that thuram underwent chondroplasty to treat patellar chondropathy. Dr Bertrand Sonnery-Cottet carried out the procedure at the Hôpital Privé Jean Mermoz in Lyon. Locatelli had his external meniscus sutured, also in Lyon, after spraining the knee against Milan. He was due to start rehabilitation the day after the operation.

Spalletti now has to rely on Douglas Luiz, Koopmeiners and new signing Pape Matar Sarr in the middle. The run opens with Venezia at 12:30 on 22 November. Omonia visit the Allianz Stadium at 21:00 on 26 November. The trip to Como follows at 20:45 on 29 November. The sequence closes with a Coppa Italia last-16 tie against Sassuolo.

Como present a sharp test. Fàbregas’s side have 23 points. They play a European fixture on 24 November, five days before they host Juventus.

The table leaves little room for slips. Juventus have 18 points from five wins, three draws and three defeats. They are 11 points behind leaders Lazio and six points off the Champions League places.

Recent findings suggest that sarr arrived on 1 September on loan from Tottenham until 30 June 2027. Juventus paid a €2.5 million fee plus €0.3 million in additional costs. The deal includes a €27.5 million permanent transfer, spread over three financial years. That becomes compulsory if certain conditions are met during 2026/27. The club describes him as a physically strong box-to-box midfielder. He has more than 100 Premier League appearances and won the 2024/25 Europa League with Spurs.

There is some relief elsewhere in the squad. Nico Gonzalez, Conceição and Cambiaso could all be available for Venezia. Yildiz hopes to return around December.

The absences make a January move for a midfielder more likely. Juventus have three targets for the window: a centre-forward, a defensive midfielder and a left-back. Pierre-Emile Højbjerg is the name for midfield, with Sørloth and Miranda also on the list, QS reported.

Sources indicate that the profile is clear. Juventus want an experienced midfielder to bridge the gap until Thuram returns and Locatelli follows later. These remain media reports rather than a club statement.

Until then, the existing group must carry the load. The Coppa Italia tie with Sassuolo is set for the Allianz Stadium in Turin on Thursday 3 December at 21:00.
